الأخبار , البحر الأحمر , الحرب بين الجيش السوداني والدعم السريع , الدول العربية , السودان , المعارضة , الولاية الشمالية , دول الجوار , سياسة 0 البرهان أكد خلال مخاطبته أهالي وادي حلفا شمالي السودان أنه لا مكان لمن وصفهم بالعملاء وادي حلفا، 21 أكتوبر 2026 – قال رئيس مجلس السيادة الانتقالي، القائد العام للجيش السوداني، عبد الفتاح البرهان، الثلاثاء، إنه لن يكون هناك مكان في السودان لمن وصفهم بالعملاء، مؤكداً رفضه لأي محاولة لفرض حكم على السودانيين من الخارج. وأفاد البرهان لدى مخاطبته حشداً جماهيرياً بمدينة وادي حلفا في الولاية الشمالية بأن «السودان مفتوح أمام جميع أبنائه، إذا أردت الاحترام تعال إلى الداخل»، وأعلن رفضه محاولات الوصول إلى السلطة عبر العمالة أو الاستقواء بالخارج. وتابع: «مافي زول بقدر يتسلط على الشعب السوداني، لا حمدوك بجي ولا قحت بتجي، زول بشيل سلاح من برة يجي يحكمنا إلا نكون مافي»، في إشارة إلى رفضه عودة القوى السياسية إلى الحكم بدعم خارجي أو فرض إرادتها على السودانيين. وجدد البرهان موقفه الرافض للتفاوض مع قوات الدعم السريع، قائلاً إن التمرد لا مجال للحوار معه، وإن الخيار أمامه هو إلقاء السلاح والاستسلام، أو مواصلة العمليات العسكرية ضده. كما وجه رسالة إلى الجهات التي قال إنها تحرض على السودان، داعياً إياها إلى الحضور إلى الداخل، ومؤكداً أن أي طرف لن يستطيع فرض إرادته على البلاد من الخارج. وشدد رئيس مجلس السيادة على أنه لا وصاية على الشعب السوداني أو الجيش، وأن اختيار من يحكم البلاد يجب أن يتم عبر الانتخابات، قائلاً إن «الرأي في النهاية للشعب السوداني». وطمأن البرهان المواطنين بشأن مستقبل البلاد، وأكد أن الدولة ستواصل مسيرتها وأن السودان سيمضي إلى الأمام، داعياً السودانيين إلى عدم الخوف أو القلق على مستقبل الدولة. وفي سياق متصل، أعرب البرهان عن شكره لجمهورية مصر العربية، مؤكداً أن المواطنين المصريين في السودان «في أمان وما عندهم مشكلة»، ومشدداً على أهمية استمرار التواصل بين البلدين وتقوية المصالح المشتركة. الكلمات: عبد الفتاح السريع , الحكومة الموازية , السودان , دارفور , دول الجوار 0 الطينة التشادية الطينة، 21 أكتوبر 2026 – قُتل، مساء الثلاثاء، 5 أشخاص بينهم اثنان من عمال الإغاثة جراء قصف جوي بطائرة مسيّرة استهدف لاجئين سودانيين داخل الأراضي التشادية بالقرب من مدينة الطينة بولاية شمال دارفور. ومنذ اندلاع الحرب في السودان في 15 أبريل 2023 فرّ آلاف المدنيين من ولايات وسط وغرب وشمال دارفور إلى الأراضي التشادية، بحثاً عن الأمان في ظل انتهاكات قوات الدعم السريع، لينضموا إلى اللاجئين السودانيين الذين لجأوا إلى تشاد منذ عام 2003 إبان الحرب التي اندلعت في دارفور خلال عهد الرئيس المعزول عمر البشير. وقال مجلس غرف الطوارئ بمحلية الطينة بولاية شمال دارفور إن «متطوعَين في العمل الإنساني وثلاثة نازحين قُتلوا جراء قصف جوي استهدف مساء الثلاثاء منطقة بامنا، فيما أصيب عدد من المدنيين بإصابات خطرة». وتقع بلدة «بامنا» داخل الأراضي التشادية، حيث لجأ إليها آلاف المواطنين السودانيين من مناطق الطينة وأمبرو وكرنوي بولاية شمال دارفور جراء الهجمات التي تشنها قوات الدعم السريع. وأفاد البيان أن القصف أسفر عن مقتل الهادي صندل عيسى، منسق غرفة طوارئ بامنا، والمتطوع آدم عمدة عرجة، عضو مكتب البرامج، إلى جانب ثلاثة من النازحين المقيمين بمراكز الإيواء في المنطقة. وأشار إلى أن عدداً من المدنيين أصيبوا بجروح خطرة جراء القصف، لافتاً إلى أن الانقطاع التام للاتصالات يزيد من صعوبة متابعة الأوضاع الميدانية والاطمئنان على المصابين. وحذّر المجلس من تداعيات استهداف المناطق المأهولة بالمدنيين ومراكز إيواء النازحين، مؤكداً أن مثل هذه الهجمات تفاقم معاناة السكان الذين أنهكتهم الحرب والنزوح، ومشدداً على ضرورة حماية المدنيين والعاملين في المجال الإنساني وضمان وصول المساعدات الإنسانية بصورة آمنة. ولم يحمّل المجلس أي جهة مسؤولية الوقوف وراء الحادثة، ولكن متطوعين في منطقة الطينة اتهموا قوات الدعم السريع بقصف اللاجئين السودانيين، ضمن موجة تصعيد جوي استهدف أماكن تجمعاتهم في المناطق الحدودية بين السودان وتشاد. وسبق أن اتُّهمت قوات الدعم السريع بتجاوز الحدود السودانية والتوغل داخل الأراضي التشادية في أكثر من ثلاث مناسبات شملت توغلات برية وهجمات على معسكرات للجيش التشادي، إلى جانب هجمات بطائرات مسيّرة استهدفت مدنيين سودانيين Báo Nhân dân • 21/10/2026 اتبع فيتنام G o o g l e أضف Vietnam.vn على G o o g l e 0 يتصاعد الدخان واللهب عقب هجوم بطائرة مسيرة في بورتسودان، شرق السودان. (صورة: THX/VNA) كان هذا أحد أكثر الهجمات دموية منذ اندلاع الصراع في السودان عام 2023. قد يعجبك أيضاً قال مسؤول إعلامي إقليمي في أبيي إن حصيلة القتلى جراء هجوم 19 أكتوبر/تشرين الأول ارتفعت من 73 إلى 153 قتيلاً. ولا تزال عمليات البحث عن الجثث وانتشالها جارية، في حين تستمر الحرائق التي اندلعت عقب الغارة الجوية في الانتشار، مما قد يزيد من عدد القتلى. أفادت مصادر دبلوماسية وشهود عيان بأن طائرة مسيرة استهدفت مستودع وقود في السوق. وكان الموقع يُستخدم سابقاً من قبل قوات الدعم السريع شبه العسكرية لإعادة تزويد وحداتها بالوقود. ووفقاً لمسؤولين في أبيي، أجبر الهجوم نحو 8000 شخص على الفرار من منازلهم. أبيي منطقة غنية بالنفط تقع بين السودان وجنوب السودان. وتطالب الدولتان بالسيادة عليها وتديرانها حالياً بشكل مشترك. وتجاور المنطقة ولاية كردفان السودانية، التي أصبحت ساحة معركة رئيسية في الصراع بين الجيش السوداني وقوات الدعم السريع. قد يعجبك أيضاً تسببت الحرب في السودان، التي اندلعت في أبريل/نيسان 2023 بين القوات المسلحة السودانية وقوات الدعم السريع، في أزمة إنسانية حادة. وقد كثّف الطرفان مؤخراً استخدامهما للطائرات المسيّرة لاستهداف المناطق الخاضعة لسيطرة الطرف الآخر. وفي أبيي، تتكرر أعمال العنف بين الجماعات العرقية والجماعات المسلحة. ويُصعّب نقص الأدوية والإمدادات الطبية ومرافق الرعاية الصحية علاج الضحايا. ويزيد الهجوم الأخير من المخاوف بشأن تأثير الحرب على المدنيين وخطر امتداد عدم الاستقرار إلى المناطق الحدودية. ethiopia.title: Prisoner of History, Not Geography
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Prisoner of History, Not Geography - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Prisoner of History, Not Geography 20 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) opinion Addis Abeba — In early October 2026, Ethiopia and Eritrea took their quarrel to the UN Security Council by letter. Addis Abeba told council members that Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 km into Tigray, which Eritrea denies. Asmara replied by calling the accusation a declaration of war and asking the council to take deterrent measures. Ethiopia also alleges that Eritrea is helping fund, mobilize, and direct armed groups in the north. Eritrea, for its part, says Addis Abeba is using its demand for sea access, along with the refrain that Ethiopia "cannot remain a prisoner of geography," as a pretext for military escalation. Officially, Ethiopia says it would pursue access through peace and dialogue. Beneath the exchange of letters lies a misunderstanding of geopolitical theory. When leaders frame Ethiopia, a country of more than 120 million people, as trapped in a landlocked cell by an accident of nature, they borrow shorthand from Tim Marshall's best-selling Prisoners of Geography . It is the kind of snappy line that makes a regional crisis sound like spatial fate. It is a compelling narrative, but it misreads physical geography. Ethiopia's landlocked condition is historical, legal, and political . That is not semantic pedantry; it dictates the cure. If a state is trapped by nature, only brute force or miraculous engineering can break its walls. If it is trapped by human choices, then diplomacy, international law, and regional trade corridors are the proper keys. What a "Prisoner of Geography" actually means Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Marshall's framework applies to immutable physical constraints: terrain that cannot be flattened, climates that cannot be negotiated with, and distances that cannot be erased. Russia is the classic case. Russia's western frontier rests on the North European Plain, a vast flat corridor from Germany to Moscow with no mountain range to stop an invader. Napoleon crossed it in 1812; Hitler in 1941. That vulnerability has driven centuries of Russian effort to push buffer zones westward. On the water, Russia has thousands of miles of coastline but few useful outlets. Murmansk stays ice-free but is hemmed in by the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap. The Black Sea fleet must pass through the Turkish-controlled Bosporus. The Baltic exits squeeze through the Danish straits, and Vladivostok is ice-affected in winter and tucked behind the Japanese archipelago. Catherine the Great's drive to the Black Sea answered this problem, and the problem has outlived her. Whether ruled by a Tsar, a Soviet commissar, or a modern president, the Kremlin keeps getting handed the same geography exam, and the water questions never get easier. This gives us a diagnostic test: a true prisoner of geography remains imprisoned no matter how many times the regime changes, the ideology shifts, or treaties are signed. Consider the rivers of Sub-Saharan Africa. The Congo and the Zambezi carry immense volumes of water, yet rapids, cataracts, and steep escarpments break them into disconnected stretches, preventing continuous navigation from the interior to the sea. Europe's navigable rivers carried goods straight to its ports. No act of parliament or diplomatic summit can persuade a waterfall to flow upstream. Applying the test to Ethiopia Ethiopia fails the test. Its topography is formidable: a volcanic highland massif carved by gorges and split by the Great Rift Valley, which made internal transport a historical challenge. But access to the Red Sea is a different spatial question. The coast is not separated from the highlands by impassable barriers, and Ethiopia has used it. Ethiopia's access to the sea has always been a matter of arrangements, not terrain. It reached the water first by the Franco-Ethiopian railway to Djibouti, which arrived in Addis Abeba in 1917, then, after the 1952 federation with Eritrea, through Assab and Massawa. Even after independence in 1993, cargo kept moving through Assab until the 1998-2000 war closed it. The land never changed. The paperwork did. Ethiopia's access to the sea has always been a matter of arrangements, not terrain." Ethiopia did not lose its coast because tectonic plates threw a tantrum or a mountain range erupted overnight. It lost the sea because of politics , the one force that can relocate a border faster than continental drift. The chain of events is long: Ottoman and Egyptian expansion along the coast; Italian colonization and the creation of Eritrea as a distinct unit; the 1952 UN federation ; the 1962 annexation under Emperor Haile Selassie; a thirty-year war of independence; the 1993 referendum ; and the breakdown of relations in 1998. Every link was a human decision. When Eritrea became independent, Assab became a foreign port, not because the earth shifted but because of a referendum that Ethiopia's own transitional government agreed to and the international community recognized. Ethiopia is not a prisoner of geography. It is a prisoner of history. Global Lessons: Bolivia, Switzerland, and international law The distinction between historical contingency and geographic destiny is well illustrated elsewhere. Bolivia lost its Pacific coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific in the 1880s. Like Ethiopia, it became landlocked through a lost war and later treaties, not because a mountain range rose between its cities and the sea. Bolivia still marks a Day of the Sea each year and keeps a navy on Lake Titicaca, a remarkable act of national memory. Yet when it took Chile to the International Court of Justice , the court ruled in 2018 that Chile had no obligation to negotiate sovereign access. Bolivia's practical economic life has gone on through transit corridors and port facilities on the Chilean and Peruvian coasts. Switzerland, an Alpine nation with no coast, moves its exports down the Rhine to Rotterdam under negotiated transit arrangements with its neighbors. The pattern is clear: where landlocked status is the product of history and borders, commercial access is solved through law, diplomacy, and shared infrastructure, not by claiming a neighbor's territory. International law reflects this. Article 125 of the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantees landlocked states a right of access to and from the sea and freedom of transit. It grants a right of transit, not a right to a sovereign coastline. The danger of misdiagnosis Misdiagnosing a political problem as geographic destiny is a dangerous policy mistake. If a nation convinces itself that it sits in a permanent cage imposed by nature, peaceful tools start to look inadequate, and force starts to look like liberation. To be fair to Addis Abeba, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed describes the quest for sea access as irreversible while stressing his commitment to diplomacy. But rhetoric about spatial entitlement has a way of outrunning the diplomacy it promises. The 1998-2000 war killed tens of thousands, devastated both economies, and ended with Ethiopia cut off from Assab, the opposite of its intended effect. Critics will say that Eritrea's own secession shows borders do change. They do, and the difference is consent. Eritrea's independence came through a referendum that Ethiopia's government accepted. Taking a port by force would set a different precedent: that population size or historical grievance justifies redrawing sovereign boundaries. On a continent whose borders were largely drawn by colonial cartographers, that principle would threaten the foundations of the African Union and, in time, Ethiopia's own boundaries. The alternatives are practical, if imperfect. Djibouti handles most of Ethiopia's trade, and diversifying through Berbera, Lamu, and Port Sudan would reduce dependence on it. Each comes with caveats: Berbera lies in Somaliland, whose status Somalia contests, and Port Sudan sits in a country at war. The strongest option is a negotiated commercial arrangement with Eritrea itself, such as port-use rights, shared infrastructure, and trade guarantees, built on the Algiers Agreement framework that both sides signed in 2000. Over-reliance on one corridor through Djibouti burdens Ethiopian businesses, creates strategic vulnerability and constrains a giant economy. Acknowledging that does not require mislabeling its cause. Russia cannot negotiate away the flat open corridor of the North European Plain, and African inland states cannot treaty away river cataracts. Ethiopia can negotiate, build, and trade its way to secure, diversified sea access. Geology may even help eventually: the Afar rift is slowly pulling Africa apart, and some geologists expect a new sea to form there in millions of years. Diplomacy is faster. Ethiopia is not locked in a natural prison. The cell was built by human history, and its door can be opened by human diplomacy. Conclusion The "prisoner of geography" narrative inherently invites military solutions, tempting leaders to enforce their will through force rather than diplomacy. Yet, territory and seaports seized at the barrel of a gun cannot deliver long-term security. True statesmanship lies in converting battlefield leverage into lasting political settlements before war becomes inevitable. Negotiation must not be a desperate last resort pursued only when ammunition is spent, and the economy has collapsed--as the Derg regime learned far too late after squandering its golden opportunities for peace. Real military maturity is measured by using power to forge peace while strong. As Scripture reminds us to remember our Creator in our youth, the optimal time to secure the Horn of Africa's future is during moments of strength. Residents who spoke to Addis Standard accuse the Somali Region Police of shooting at the child and killing her instantly. Meanwhile, residents from the Somali side told Addis Standard that the girl was killed in crossfire between the two sides. Following the incident, elders and security officials reportedly agreed on Monday to remove the Somali Region's flag. However, the decision prompted demonstrations by Somali resident particularly in Kebele 02 on Tuesday that disrupted transport services and forced businesses and bus stations to close amid security fears. Mallicha Diida, a resident of Moyale's Kebele 02, told Addis Standard that the latest incident was part of a recurring cycle of violence in the town. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines "In Moyale, human blood has been spilled year after year. Last Sunday, when Somali Regional administration bodies opened a new mayor's office around Kebele 02 and hoisted the Somali Region flag, this act deeply angered many people," he said. Mallicha said gunfire subsequently broke out between Oromia militia members and Somali Region police, prompting the immediate intervention of the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), which stopped the exchange. He alleged that Somali Region police shot and killed the 13-year-old girl, describing the incident as an act of "cruelty and lawlessness". He said the officers had killed the child rather than hold those responsible for any alleged wrongdoing accountable, claiming they accused her of throwing stones at them. A resident on the Somali side offered a different account, telling Addis Standard that the Somali-side Moyale town administration had merely relocated its office from its previous premises to a new location. "When they attempted to bring office equipment and hoist the flag, Oromia Region militias opened fire on the Somali Region police to prevent them from succeeding. The young girl was killed in the middle of this, but Somali Region security forces did not target or kill that child," the resident said, rejecting allegations that Somali Region forces were responsible for her death. During an interview with the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), the Prime Minister said Eritrean cities were once thriving economic centers when Eritrea was part of Ethiopia. However, these assets have significantly deteriorated since Eritrea's secession, with some cities losing much of their former urban character. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Recalling that Eritrea had more than 300 industries during that period, the Premier said the region had a substantial industrial base, contrasting its former economic strength with what he described as its present decline. Citing Asmara, PM Abiy said the capital had become smaller than many developing Ethiopian cities such as Arba Minch and Jigjiga. Speaking about the Red Sea port cities of Massawa and Assab, the Prime Minister said their economic activity had declined significantly, leaving their potential largely underutilized. "Massawa has been emptied, while Assab has been reduced to a ghost town," Prime Minister Abiy said. The Prime Minister attributed the situation to the Eritrean government's failure to prioritize development and institution-building, adding that its policies had instead drawn the country into serving the interests of forces opposed to Ethiopia. He said Eritreans, whom he described as industrious and welcoming, were now facing displacement and hardship, underscoring that external factors supporting confrontation would not resolve the country's underlying challenges. Such involvement, the Premier said, offers no lasting solution to Eritrea's problems, as those supporting confrontation are more likely to provide ammunition than contribute to addressing the country's difficulties. He stressed that friendship, good neighborliness and development cooperation remain the viable path forward, noting that decades of experience have demonstrated the limitations of alternative approaches. The Prime Minister warned that continued disregard for calls to pursue partnership and development, rather than allowing the region to become an arena for external rivalries, could have serious consequences. ethiopia.title: Eritrea's Migration Economy - Can the Nation Survive Without Forced Remittance?
ethiopia.content: Eritrea's Migration Economy - Can the Nation Survive Without Forced Remittance? - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Eritrea's Migration Economy - Can the Nation Survive Without Forced Remittance? 20 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) October 20, 2026 (ENA) Britain's October 2026 ultimatum to Eritrea exposed a long-standing contradiction at the heart of Isaias Afwerki's regime. The Asmara administration promotes self-reliance while rejecting fixed national budgets and external dependence. Yet, its system is sustained by the very forces it claims to transcend: indefinite national service drives emigration, while remittances from Eritreans abroad help finance the system that compels them to leave. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood announced that Eritrea faces a total visa ban for its nationals unless Asmara resumes cooperation on the return of failed asylum seekers and foreign national offenders. Preferential processing for officials has already been withdrawn, and diplomats have been placed under travel limits outside London. This announcement came at a moment when Eritreans formed the largest nationality among small-boat arrivals in the year to June 2026--roughly 5,875 recorded arrivals, or about 18 percent of the total--and ranked second in overall asylum claims, with initial grant rates near 83-84 percent. Although Eritrea dismissed the pressure as a "dismissible political gimmick," the sequence of events requires a closer examination of a political economy that has organized continuous emigration into a remittance resource. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn That political economy, controlled by Shabia under President Isaias Afwerki since independence, rests on three interlocking pillars: indefinite national service, party ownership of the command economy, and the systematic capture of external financial flows. While appearing distinct, these pillars function as a single mechanism that converts the population into both a captive labor force at home and a source of finance abroad. This framework structured itself around the continuous extraction of value from that emigration, yielding a sustained regime monopoly. Way back in 1997, Eritrea ratified a constitution that has remained unimplemented for nearly three decades. In 2001, independent media outlets were shut down after senior party figures called for democratic elections and constitutional enforcement. As a result, what was once framed as temporary wartime mobilization hardened into a permanent state architecture in which citizenship itself was redefined as an obligation rather than a right. Although national service was formally limited to 18 months under Proclamation 82/1995, it has operated without an end date since the 1998-2000 border war. Secondary school students complete their final year at the Sawa military training center before being assigned to military or civilian roles that can last for decades, earning a meager stipend of 450 to 500 Nakfa a month--roughly 30 USD. Conditions like these are what the UN Commission of Inquiry characterized as "slavery-like," linking them to arbitrary detention and the collective punishment of families. Such practices drive continuous emigration, where the outflow is not a policy failure but rather a deliberate revenue stream. While resident population estimates hover around 3.6 million, diaspora figures range from roughly 600,000 to 900,000 registered migrants and refugees, with up to one-third of the Eritrean-born population living outside the country. According to UNHCR data for the end of 2025, there were roughly 555,000 refugees plus more than 118,000 asylum seekers--totaling approximately 670,000-679,000 people of concern--with new asylum applications in 2025 alone exceeding 53,000. Although the formal economy remains dominated by Shabia-linked enterprises and the state, private-sector activity outside small family trade is constrained by currency controls, licensing restrictions, and the national-service labor regime. The decisive resource is human capital exported and then taxed; most household survival depends on external transfers estimated at 200 to 300 million USD annually--equivalent to roughly 30 percent of Eritrea's GDP. These flows keep households solvent in an environment of limited domestic opportunity, while a parallel 2 percent diaspora tax is levied on Eritreans abroad and collected through embassies and informal networks. Economic ownership is concentrated in party-controlled structures: the Hidri Trust functions as the central holding vehicle for Shabia's commercial interests, the Red Sea Trading Corporation holds an effective monopoly on significant imports and serves as a primary channel for foreign exchange, construction firms such as Segen and Bidho execute major works frequently using national-service labor, and Himbol Financial Services manages remittances and related transactions. State banks exist, yet the party retains parallel financial channels outside conventional budgetary oversight, amidst no comprehensive national budget having been published since independence. This dual extraction reduces the need for productive employment creation and creates a closed loop in which indefinite national service and political controls generate flight, which in turn generates remittances and state revenue. When compared to the official doctrine of self-reliance that Eritrea follows--which rejects aid dependency while treating citizens as both free labor and external financiers--isolation from conventional multilateral finance is justified, while political pluralism is framed as a threat to national unity and sovereignty. This produces a distinctive equilibrium in which political power is monopolized, and the regime's authority on budgets and the precise size of party holdings stay outside public scrutiny. Eritrea's political economy has converted a significant fraction of its population into a transnational resource, where labor is extracted under coercive conditions while the diaspora supplies foreign exchange, producing an equilibrium of repression and economic stagnation. Consequently, host states are left to absorb the social and fiscal costs, as the ruling Shabia system externalizes those costs while capturing the financial returns. Eritrea's migration economy is therefore not an unintended by-product of isolation, but the operating logic of a political order that converts its people into the principal resource keeping the regime intact. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Signs Second-Phase LNG Development Deal for Ogaden Gas Field - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Signs Second-Phase LNG Development Deal for Ogaden Gas Field 20 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Chinese companies GCL Group and Jurong Group have signed an agreement to develop the second phase of a liquefied natural gas (LNG) project at Ethiopia's Calub gas field in the Somali Region, as the government seeks to expand commercial use of the country's natural gas reserves. The agreement, signed on 16 October at the Ministry of Mines in Addis Abeba in the presence of Mines Minister Alemtsehay Paulos, covers engineering, construction and natural gas liquefaction and processing services. It follows a strategic cooperation framework signed by the two companies in May 2026 and the commissioning of the project's first phase in October 2025. According to Seetao, the first phase consists of a modular LNG facility designed to process 200,000 cubic metres of natural gas daily, producing approximately 50,000 metric tonnes of LNG annually, primarily for domestic industrial consumers. The second phase is intended to increase production and serve international markets, although the companies have not disclosed the contract value, additional processing capacity or completion timeline. The agreement comes amid renewed efforts to commercialise the Ogaden Basin's gas resources after years of delays. In March 2026, GCL and Dangote Group signed a reported $4.2 billion , 25-year gas supply agreement for a urea fertiliser complex in Gode, with plans to transport gas from Calub through a pipeline of approximately 108-110 kilometres. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Poly-GCL, associated with GCL's wider corporate group, has operated in the basin since 2013 under production-sharing agreements covering the Calub and Hilala fields. Ethiopia's government terminated the company's contracts in September 2022 following disputes over capital registration, outstanding fees and delays in development, before reversing the decision in June 2024. In August 2022, Ethiopia received its first gas reserves certificate, confirming an estimated seven trillion cubic feet of natural gas in the Ogaden Basin, according to a study by Netherland, Sewell & Associates. Despite the renewed investment push, export arrangements for the LNG project remain unclear. Ethiopia is landlocked, and earlier proposals to transport gas to Djibouti for export have not resulted in a publicly confirmed export route for the second phase. The agreement's financing, delivery schedule and intended international buyers have also not been announced. Read the original article on Addis Standard . The swearing-in follows the certification of the September 30 parliamentary election results by Somalia’s Supreme Court, which confirmed the Justice and Solidarity Party (JSP) secured 78 of the 99 seats in the assembly. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the electoral timetable , the court stated that no legal challenges had been filed against the results, clearing the way for the new legislature to convene. According to the schedule published by the National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (NIEBC), candidates for Speaker and Deputy Speakers submitted their applications on Wednesday, October 21. Campaign speeches and the speakership vote are scheduled for Thursday, October 22. The timeline then shifts to the executive. Applications for the regional presidency and vice-presidency will open on Friday, October 23, with candidate speeches and the final vote set for Saturday, October 24. A Parliament of Unprecedented Composition The September 30 vote marked the first time residents of Hirshabelle directly elected both regional lawmakers and local councillors, replacing the previous system of indirect clan-based selection. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the election results , 114,633 people cast ballots across 10 districts, with 112,466 votes declared valid. The JSP’s victory was overwhelming. The party received more than 88,000 votes, giving it nearly four-fifths of the seats in the new assembly. Karaama finished second with six seats, followed by Iftiin Qaran with five and Sincad with three. In the simultaneous local council elections, JSP won 158 of the 222 seats contested, further consolidating its control over Hirshabelle’s political institutions. The Unresolved Hiiraan Question While the procedural path to a new administration is clear, the political foundation remains contested. The JSP has nominated incumbent President Ali Abdullahi Hussein Guudlaawe for another term, a decision that has sharpened a long-running power-sharing dispute between the Hawadle community of Hiiraan and the Abgaal community of Middle Shabelle. Hirshabelle Vice President Yusuf Ahmed Hagar Dabageed, a Hawadle politician, has publicly accused President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud of reneging on a promise to return the regional presidency to the Hawadle clan. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the JSP nomination dispute , Dabageed stated that when he asked the president about his own candidacy, the president replied that he would give the position to Guudlaawe instead. The dispute has also raised questions about the inclusivity of the electoral process in Hiiraan. Prior to the parliamentary vote, Dabageed warned that elections could not proceed in the region without a political agreement involving traditional elders and local stakeholders. While voting did take place in Beledweyne, the underlying grievances remain unresolved. As reported in FTL Somalia’s analysis of the Hawadle political crisis , the community’s sense of abandonment has pushed some leaders toward dangerous alternatives, including reported contacts with Al-Shabaab . The JSP has selected former Hiiraan governor Abdifatah Hassan Afrah as its vice-presidential candidate, pairing him with Guudlaawe in the forthcoming leadership election. The arrangement is intended to balance the ticket, but it does not address the Hawadle demand for the presidency itself. Critical Note The swearing-in of Hirshabelle’s new parliament is a procedural milestone, and the direct election of lawmakers represents a genuine shift from the indirect selection systems that have governed Somali regional politics for years. The JSP’s victory is decisive, and the party now controls the institutions through which Hirshabelle’s next leadership will be chosen. But the parliament that convened in Jowhar on Tuesday does not represent a political consensus. It represents the outcome of an election that the JSP dominated, in a state where the ruling party at the federal level has openly backed its preferred candidates for regional office. The Hawadle community’s demand for the presidency, articulated by the regional vice president and supported by traditional elders, has not been resolved. It has been overruled by the arithmetic of the JSP’s 78-seat majority. Guudlaawe will almost certainly be re-elected on Saturday. The question is whether his new mandate will be seen as legitimate by the constituencies that feel excluded from the process. A parliament elected directly is a step forward. A presidency elected by a parliament that was itself the product of a lopsided contest is a different matter. The next five days will produce a government. They will not, by themselves, produce the political trust that Hirshabelle has lacked since its formation. According to reports from Somali media, two candidates are contesting the presidency and two are contesting the vice-presidency. Each addressed the House of Representatives, outlining their policy priorities and urging members to support their bids. The election is scheduled for October 22, following the timetable announced by the National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (NIEBC). As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the electoral schedule , the NIEBC set the candidate speeches for October 21 and the final vote for October 22. The Candidates and the Contest The presidential race is headed by Liban Ahmed Hassan, the sole candidate nominated by the Justice and Solidarity Party (JSP), and Abduqadir Abdullahi Diriye Adawe of the SINCAD Party. Liban Hassan received his candidate certificate earlier this week, clearing the final procedural hurdle before the vote, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of his certification [citation:2]. He has pledged to prioritise transparency, security, economic development, and inclusive governance. During his campaign, he outlined a three-point agenda that included ridding Galmudug of Al-Shabaab within six months, spearheading reconciliation, and delivering rapid development, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the JSP campaign . Adawe was nominated by SINCAD in July 2026, promising to focus on security, reconciliation, and economic development. He said his administration would seek to improve access to education and healthcare, develop infrastructure, and create opportunities for young people, women, and businesses, as reported in The Standard’s coverage of his nomination . A Vote Overshadowed by Exclusion While the candidates made their pitches, the political context of the election remains deeply contested. The parliament that will decide the presidency was elected in a court-ordered rerun on September 30, after the Supreme Court annulled the original July 30 vote for procedural and constitutional violations. The rerun excluded the Towfiiq political organisation, the party that had successfully brought the legal challenge leading to the annulment. The NIEBC stated that Towfiiq had failed to meet the deadline for submitting candidate lists, a decision the party has contested. The JSP holds 67 of the 89 seats in the assembly, and its candidates also hold the Speaker and both Deputy Speaker positions, as reported in SONNA’s coverage of the parliamentary leadership vote . With that majority, Liban Hassan’s election is widely expected, making Adawe’s candidacy a symbolic challenge rather than a competitive threat. Critical Note The candidate speeches are a required procedural step in Galmudug’s electoral calendar, and the fact that multiple candidates are contesting the presidency and vice-presidency provides at least a veneer of competition. But the outcome of Thursday’s vote is not in doubt. The JSP’s two-thirds majority in a parliament elected without its principal challenger means that Liban Hassan’s path to the presidency is effectively assured. The deeper problem is not who wins on Thursday. It is whether the winner will govern with a mandate that extends beyond the JSP’s parliamentary bloc. The exclusion of Towfiiq, the controversy surrounding the NIEBC’s neutrality, and the federal government’s overt backing of the JSP candidate have all been documented. These are not minor procedural complaints. They speak to the legitimacy of the entire process. Liban Hassan has promised to heal clan divisions and defeat Al-Shabaab within six months. Those are ambitious commitments for any leader. They will be particularly difficult to fulfill for a president whose election will be seen by significant constituencies as the product of a process from which meaningful competition was removed. The speeches on Wednesday offered visions of reform and development. Whether those visions can be realized will depend on whether the new president can reach beyond the chamber that elected him and address the grievances that made this election so contested in the first place. somalia.title: Trump’s Obsession With Somalia Isn’t Just Racist. It’s Been Lethal. - The Intercept
somalia.content: Trump’s Obsession With Somalia Isn’t Just Racist. It’s Been Lethal. It’s Been Lethal. Beyond targeting Rep. Ilhan Omar, the Trump administration has killed, arrested, deported, and demonized Somalis at home and abroad. Nick Turse October 21 2026, 6:00 a.m. ET Share Copy link Share on Facebook Share on Bluesky Share on X Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., in her office on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on Dec. 10, 2025. Photo: Demetrius Freeman/The Washington Post via Getty Images The Trump administration is waging a multi-pronged war on Somali people, painting them as criminals, murderers, and terrorists and using multiple federal agencies to target them at home and abroad. The campaign includes military attacks in Somalia, as well as arrests, deportations, and the weaponization of federal law enforcement agencies against immigrants and the Somali American community in the United States, including the recent use of Homeland Security agents as a goon squad to target Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar. In his second term, President Donald Trump has routinely cast Somalia as lawless and Somalis as violent . Meanwhile, his administration has, largely without public knowledge, killed hundreds of people in Somalia, claiming they belong to terror groups. Trump personally ordered the death of a Somali man within days of regaining the White House, according to his counterterrorism czar Sebastian Gorka. The administration claimed, without offering any evidence, that the man was connected with the Islamic State terror group. Trump has sought to do the same with Omar. Homeland Security agents raided Omar’s Washington, D.C., home last Monday, three weeks before the midterms , in which she is seeking reelection. The Trump administration reportedly launched the investigation to build a case to strip Omar of her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deport her. (Omar fled war in Somalia with her family when she was 8 years old, later immigrated to the U.S. as a refugee , and became a citizen in 2000.) The administration has also issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including to some of Omar’s relatives. On Monday, conservative media outlets reported that federal prosecutors obtained Omar’s DNA as part of their investigation. “This is what happens in a dictatorship. The leader identifies his political, ethnic and religious enemies, and his agents scramble to do his bidding and make him happy,” Zaynab Mohamed, a Somali immigrant who represents Minneapolis in Minnesota’s state Senate, told The Intercept. “Representative Omar is the latest subject where Trump identifies the target and his minions go looking for a crime. The cases always fall apart, and this one will, too.” Related DHS Was Designed as a Weapon Trump claimed not to have ordered the raid, but throughout his second term, his Justice Department has repeatedly targeted his political enemies — from New York’s attorney general , to the former head of the FBI, to members of the Federal Reserve. “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ,” Trump said to reporters. “I have nothing to do with it.” Omar called it “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” She added: “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.” Omar’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment from The Intercept. With the Somali community , Trump found a target that he could attack with Islamophobic, racist, and xenophobic rhetoric , without incurring much mainstream backlash, said Jaylani Hussein, the executive director of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations. “As immigrants, Muslims, and — most importantly — Black people, it’s the trifecta,” he told The Intercept. “None of us expected the scale and level of the vitriol. But despite this, it’s at the point that the traditional media almost ignore the attacks on the Somali-American community because it’s not a large constituency. Trump says these things, and people just move on.” Most Read Inside ICE, Officials Question String of Trump Admin “Midterm Panic Moves” Karl Loftus Lockheed Martin Showered Susan Collins With Cash as F-35 Program Hit Turbulence Noah Hurowitz President Apocalypse Tom Engelhardt Trump’s War on Somalia Over the last decade, Trump has overseen the killing of as many as 1,500 Somalis in more than 400 attacks, according to a count by New America, a D.C.-based think tank. During his second term alone, the Trump administration has conducted more than 200 airstrikes in Somalia, including close to 90 this year, claiming to target terrorists. The U.S. military has been at war in Somalia for almost a quarter-century, conducting air attacks and commando raids aimed at the terrorist group al-Shabab as well as the Islamic State group, while the CIA and special operators created local proxy forces to conduct low-profile operations on behalf of America. At the same time, the U.S. has provided Somalia with billions of dollars in counterterrorism assistance. Related U.S. Conducts “Largest Airstrike in the History of the World” (Sort Of) U.S. attacks in Somalia have skyrocketed during Trump’s terms in office. From 2007 to 2017, under the administrations of George W. Bush and Barack Obama, the U.S. military carried out 59 declared airstrikes in Somalia. The Biden administration conducted 51 declared strikes over four years. During Trump’s six years in office, the U.S. has launched more than 400 attacks against purported militants. The U.S. rarely offers any evidence that those killed are members of terrorist groups, much less leaders. A New America analysis found militant leaders comprised just 1.7 percent of those killed. Africa Command refused to provide requested evidence that any of those killed in airstrikes in Somalia this year were militants. “All U.S. strikes in Somalia are conducted in close coordination partners [sic] against designated terror groups,” an AFRICOM spokesperson told The Intercept by email. “Trump has conducted more drone strikes in Somalia than Bush, Obama, and Biden combined. And so many civilians have died,” historian Elizabeth Schmidt, the author of “Foreign Intervention in Africa After the Cold War: Sovereignty, Responsibility, and the War on Terror,” told The Intercept. “They were often just young men living in an area where it was easy to label them jihadis. And it turns out they had nothing to do with terrorism.” The U.S. claims that it has only killed six civilians over almost two decades of war in Somalia. A count by the airstrike monitoring group Airwars put the number at as much as 2,600 percent higher . A 2023 investigation by The Intercept determined, for example, that a drone attack in Somalia during Trump’s first term killed at least three, and possibly five, civilians, including 22-year-old Luul Dahir Mohamed and her 4-year-old daughter Mariam Shilow Muse. At the time of the attack, the U.S. announced it had killed “ five terrorists ” and that “no civilians were killed in this airstrike.” Trump calls Somalia a “third-world” or “ fourth-world nation ,” says that it “ stinks ,” and disparaged Somalis who come to the U.S., saying “we’re going to go the wrong way if we keep taking in garbage into our country.” His most xenophobic consigliere also claims Somalia is responsible for violence that has caused people to flee the country. “The entire Somali refugee program is predicated on a lie,” wrote Trump’s deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, Stephen Miller, late last year. “Destroying your own country does not give you the right to become a citizen in ours.” But this faux history disregards America’s decadeslong role in fomenting violence in Somalia and destabilizing the country. “The presence of Somalis in the U.S. has a lot to do with U.S. wars in Somalia.” A casualty of the Cold War geopolitics that led to widespread conflict, political repression, and millions of deaths across the developing world, Somalia has experienced persistent political instability and strife since the late 1960s. In recent decades, the country has suffered civil war, famine, droughts, a longtime al-Shabab insurgency, and persistent humanitarian crises. Related Who Could Have Predicted the U.S. War in Somalia Would Fail? The Pentagon. Over the last quarter century, the U.S. has intensified conflict in Somalia through direct attacks; training, funding, and running proxy forces; and funneling in weapons and other military assistance to one side of a civil war. As early as 2007, the Pentagon was aware that there were fundamental flaws with U.S. military operations in the Horn of Africa, and Somalia devolved into another forever war stalemate. This has continued, despite the record number of airstrikes in Somalia under Trump. Before Trump took office, in 2016, Islamist militants in Somalia killed 4,281 people , according to the Africa Center for Strategic Studies, a Pentagon research institution. By August, this year’s total hit 6,731 deaths, a 57 percent increase. An analysis by the Costs of War project at Brown University found that instead of eliminating militant groups, the U.S. counterterrorism campaign in Somalia was “ensuring that the conflict continues in perpetuity.” An AFRICOM spokesperson said the command’s “operational focus remains on working with partners to degrade terrorist organizations to create the space required for Somali-led governance and stability.” But Trump claims Somalia has no government , no military , and is “ not even a country .” “ They weren’t coming because they wanted a better job. It’s because they feared for their lives and their children’s lives.” The Intercept interviewed people displaced by the forever war in a camp on the outskirts of Somalia’s capital, Mogadishu, in 2023. “We had to leave because of the drought and the conflict,” a mother of seven told this reporter. She was one of more than a dozen women from the Lower Shabelle region of southwest Somalia who spoke to The Intercept after fleeing the front lines of an offensive by the U.S.-backed Somali government against al-Shabab. Since Trump first took office, the number of Somalis forced from their homes has almost doubled from 2.4 million to 4.4 million. “I don’t think most Americans realize that the presence of Somalis in the U.S. has a lot to do with U.S. wars in Somalia. U.S. military intervention made a bad situation worse. This led to a surge of refugees and asylum-seekers to the U.S.,” said Schmidt. “They weren’t coming because they wanted a better job. It’s because they feared for their lives and their children’s lives.” During Trump’s first term, his administration acknowledged “ the ongoing armed conflict ” as a reason to extend temporary protected status — which grants legal status, work authorization, and protection from deportation — to Somalis in the U.S., noting the security situation was “fragile and volatile, with ongoing armed conflict among government forces, clan militias, African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) troops, and al-Shabaab.” We’re independent of corporate interests — and powered by members. Delivered to you. I'm in Bringing the War Home Despite the increase in violence, according to Pentagon statistics, the administration terminated Somalia’s TPS designation earlier this year. More than 1,000 Somali asylum-seekers have been ordered deported since February; more than half the deportation orders involve Somalis living in Minnesota, a nearly tenfold increase from 2025, according to a Minnesota Star Tribune investigation. About 84,000 of the 260,000 people of Somali descent in the U.S. live in the Minneapolis–St. Paul area, according to the Census Bureau’s annual American Community Survey. The overwhelming majority are American citizens. Almost 58 percent were born in the U.S. and 87 percent of foreign-born Somalis are naturalized citizens. Related Unnamed Source in Viral Minnesota Somali Fraud Video Is Right-Wing Lobbyist Who Called Muslims “Demons” The administration targeted that Somali community during a violent immigration crackdown in and around Minneapolis known as “ Operation Metro Surge ” during late 2025 and early 2026. “I don’t want them in our country,” Trump said in December 2025. The next month, he said: “Every one of them should be forced to leave this country, including Ilhan Omar.” During Metro Surge, federal agents shot and killed protesters Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti . They, like Omar and hundreds of drone strike victims in Somalia, were labeled as terrorists by the administration without providing evidence. “If the president can threaten to denaturalize and deport a member of Congress, no one is safe.” During Trump’s second term, Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have also arrested hundreds of Somali people, with reports of assault and mistreatment at the hands of federal agents. Trump recently seemed to call for vigilante violence and threatened to back it with federal force. “The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants,” Trump posted on Truth Social earlier this month. “The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing. They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back! If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Hussein, of CAIR-MN, said Trump’s rhetoric was endangering the Somali community. “Every few weeks, he’s literally going on a tirade. And I don’t think he’s ever spoken about other people the same way. He literally put out the message saying, ‘go fight them. I’ll come and help’ on social media,” he told The Intercept. “We’ve seen bullying. We’ve dealt with harassment. We’ve have some assaults.” Related Trump Is Targeting Ilhan Omar. Where’s the Elite Media Outrage? Trump has routinely demonized Somalis by tying the broader community to a high-profile fraud case : the alleged theft of $250 million from a pandemic-era program that provided food for children. The former leader of Feeding Our Future, the nonprofit at the center of the case, is white, although most of the defendants in the related cases are of Somali descent. “The Somalians, they’re crooked as hell,” Trump ranted at a Cabinet meeting in May, with the administration offering escalating and unverified claims, including reference to a “ $19 billion Somali fraud scandal .” The Trump administration’s effort to denaturalize and deport Omar is part of a broader push to strip naturalized Americans of their citizenship, with those of Somali descent specifically singled out. “I would do it in a heartbeat if they were dishonest,” Trump said in an Oval Office interview earlier this year. “I think that many of the people that came in from Somalia, they hate our country.” Trump’s border czar Tom Homan said on Saturday that he had been “told they have a strong case” against Omar. “Of course, if you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody. We’ve done it before,” he told Fox News. The rarely used denaturalization statute has been most famously employed to strip citizenship from Nazi war criminals , like John Demjanjuk, a former death camp guard and retired U.S. autoworker convicted on 28,060 counts of being an accessory to murder. Mohamed, who in 2022 became the first Somali woman elected to the Minnesota Senate, called out Trump’s push to expel Omar as a grave threat to the country. “If the president can threaten to denaturalize and deport a member of Congress, no one is safe,” she told The Intercept. “This is a test of our democracy, and even Republicans should be speaking out about it. If we don’t defend the rights of Ilhan Omar, Somali-Americans, immigrants, and Trump’s political targets, we lose everything.” Share Copy link Share on Facebook Share on Bluesky Share on X Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT. What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government. This is not hyperbole. Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation. Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.” The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. somalia.content: Hormuud Telecom hosts fifth Somali Success Story Forum focused on healthcare sector Latest Headlines Hormuud Telecom hosts fifth Somali Success Story Forum focused on healthcare sector Tigray rebels claim to have killed over 1,500 Ethiopian soldiers as PM Abiy Ahmed warns Eritrea Somalia: Puntland Health Minister Inspects Dhahar Hospital During Regional Tour Christiane Amanpour to Leave CNN in 2027 After 43 Years Somalia’s Opposition Alliance to Hold Key Political Talks in Nairobi, Kenya Advertise with us Home News Puntland Somalia World Sports Press Releases Somaliland Videos Opinion Contact Privacy Policy English Somali Hormuud Telecom hosts fifth Somali Success Story Forum focused on healthcare sector Omar Nor, Chief Editor GAROWE ONLINE Posted On 21-10-2026, 09:30AM MOGADISHU, Somalia — Somalia’s leading telecommunications company Hormuud Telecom on Tuesday hosted the fifth edition of the Somalia’s Success Story Forum (BGS26) in Mogadishu, bringing together around 350 participants to discuss investment in healthcare and ways to improve medical services in the country. Held at Jazeera Hotel under the theme “Towards a Healthy Somalia”, the forum focused on healthcare investment, expanding access to medical services and addressing gaps in infrastructure and service delivery. Somalia’s Health Minister, Dr Ali Haji Adam, who officially opened the event, said investment in healthcare was essential to building a healthy society and a developed nation. He welcomed the focus on health, saying the country needed to recognise progress, confront persistent challenges and work collectively towards better medical services. "Investing in healthcare is not merely a financial commitment, but an investment in building a healthy society and a developed nation," said Dr. Ali Haji Adan, Somalia's Minister of Health, commending the convening of the forum. In his keynote speech, Hormuud Telecom Chairman Ahmed Mohamed Yusuf said healthcare was chosen as this year’s forum theme because of its importance to Somali society. He praised health workers’ efforts and said the forum aimed to recognise their contributions, strengthen public confidence in local healthcare and encourage hospitals to expand specialised services. “We chose to focus on healthcare in Somalia this year because of its vital importance to people’s lives. We commend Somalia’s healthcare professionals for their dedication and the progress they have made in advancing the country’s health sector. We organised this forum to recognise their contributions, encourage their continued efforts, and strengthen public confidence in our country’s healthcare services,” Yusuf said. The Minister of Planning, Investment and Economic Development, Hon. Mohamud Abdirahman Benabene, commended Somalia’s Success Story Forum (BGS26), highlighting its importance to the Somali people and Hormuud Telecom’s role in organising the forum. The Minister also emphasised the importance of healthcare in advancing social development and building a healthy nation. Communications and Technology Minister Mohamed Aden Moallim Ali said technology and innovation could improve access to healthcare and support the development of a modern, sustainable health system. Senator Dufle called for a unified organisation representing Somali doctors to help coordinate and improve medical services nationwide. He also conveyed congratulations from Senate Speaker Abdi Hashi Abdullahi to Somalia’s Success Story Forum (BGS26). Somalia’s first Cancer specialist Hussein Hassan Abshir addressed the burden of cancer in Somalia. He claimed that 80 percent of Somalis travelling to India for medical treatment were found to have cancer at an advanced stage when treatment was no longer possible. The figure was not independently verified. Yasin Mohamud Ibar, chairman of the Somali Chamber of Commerce and Industry, called for stronger cooperation between the government and private sector, saying partnerships could help deliver quality, affordable healthcare that people could access more easily. A key part of Somalia’s Success Story Forum (BGS26) was a panel discussion on building healthcare services that are affordable, accessible, and equitable and of high quality. The discussion examined in depth the challenges hindering improvements in Somalia’s healthcare services and explored potential solutions for the future. Deputy Prime Minister Jibril Abdirashid Haji formally closed the forum, praising its organisation and Hormuud Telecom’s role in supporting community initiatives and the development of essential services. Hormuud organises the annual Somalia’s Success Story Forum to promote innovation, investment and development by bringing together government officials, businesses, experts and development partners. This year’s event focused on strengthening Somalia’s healthcare system. The registration was conducted in coordination with the National Commission for Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons (NCRI). NIRA’s Deputy Director General, Abdirahman Said Ahmed, visited the NCRI center where the returnees were being processed, noting that the authority prioritizes issuing identification to citizens returning to the country to ease their social reintegration and access to services. The exercise is the latest phase in Somalia’s expanding national ID system, which has become the primary mechanism for citizens to access banking, education, healthcare, and domestic travel. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the eAqoonsi digital ID launch , NIRA has also introduced a mobile application allowing citizens to carry their National ID digitally, with the same legal validity as the physical card. The Returnee Pipeline The registration of Yemen returnees is part of a larger repatriation effort. In early October 2026, the Somali government repatriated 160 nationals from Yemen, including 59 women and children. Some had lived in Yemen for decades, while others were born there and were arriving in Somalia for the first time, as reported in Hiiraan Online’s coverage of the repatriation . NCRI Commissioner Liban Abdi Egal said the returnees were received at an integration center where they received medical screening, registration, identification cards, and assistance to reach their home areas. He noted that many Somalis remain in Yemen, including some registered as refugees with UNHCR, and that the number returning could rise. The context of their departure is grim. Thousands of Somalis have been stranded in Yemen, many living in makeshift homes in Aden’s “Little Mogadishu” and struggling to find work. A UN Refugee Agency survey found that 56 percent of repatriated Somalis cited a lack of income opportunities in Yemen as their primary reason for returning, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Somali migrants in Yemen . The National ID as a Gatekeeper The registration of returnees reflects a significant policy shift in Somalia’s approach to identity and service delivery. Starting in January 2026, access to key services, including opening a bank account and domestic travel, has been linked to possession of a national ID. The Central Bank of Somalia has mandated that all individuals seeking to open or renew bank accounts must present a valid National ID card, and the Ministry of Trade and Industry requires the ID for business registration. For returnees, this creates both an opportunity and an obstacle. The ID is the key that unlocks financial inclusion, formal employment, and social protection. Without it, reintegration is practically impossible. NIRA’s mobile registration teams have attempted to reach displaced populations, with a Baidoa pilot enrolling over 38,000 internally displaced persons at a cost of under one dollar per registration, as documented by UNDP Somalia . But the standard registration process can still present barriers for those lacking documentation or the ability to pay fees. Critical Note The registration of Yemen returnees is a practical necessity. Without identification, these citizens cannot open bank accounts, enroll their children in school, access healthcare, or travel freely within their own country. NIRA’s presence at the NCRI center is a recognition that reintegration begins with legal identity, and that the state has an obligation to provide it. But the policy of linking essential services to the national ID raises questions that the government has not fully addressed. For returnees who have spent years or decades abroad, the documentation required to verify their identity may be unavailable. For the poorest and most vulnerable, even nominal fees can be prohibitive. NIRA has attempted to address this through mobile registration and fee waivers in some cases, but the system’s reach is not universal. The risk is that the ID, intended as a tool of inclusion, becomes another barrier for those least able to overcome it. The returnees from Yemen are a test case. They arrive with nothing, having fled a country that offered them no future. If the state can register them, provide them with identity, and connect them to services, it will demonstrate that the national ID system is more than a bureaucratic exercise. If it cannot, the returnees will join the millions of displaced Somalis for whom legal identity remains an aspiration rather than a reality. The registration exercise this week is a start. It is not a guarantee of successful reintegration. The meeting focused on improving cooperation among government agencies, strengthening passenger safety, and advancing the clearance of designated facilities near the facility. The minister emphasized the need to expedite the evacuation plan for structures slated for relocation or demolition, describing Aden Adde as a vital entry point and an important symbol of Somalia’s international connectivity. The inspection was attended by the State Minister for Transport and Civil Aviation and other senior officials. A Pattern with Precedent The government’s push to clear structures around the airport is not new. The facility’s location within Mogadishu’s urban fabric has long presented security challenges, particularly given the persistent threat from Al-Shabaab , which has targeted the airport and the surrounding area with mortars in the past. What is notable about the current plan is its resonance with a broader, well-documented pattern of forced evictions and land seizures in Mogadishu. A Heritage Institute for Policy Studies report published in October 2026 found that between 2017 and September 2026, 2,136,420 people were evicted across Somalia, with 64 percent of those evictions occurring in the Benadir region, which encompasses the capital. The report documents a shift in the nature of evictions . In 2021, only 11 percent of evictions from Mogadishu’s displacement camps occurred on government-owned land. By 2025, that figure had risen to 44 percent. The state has transitioned from bystander to evictor, with demolitions often conducted without adequate notice, consultation, or compensation. In August 2026, violence erupted in Mogadishu’s Tookiyo neighbourhood when government forces clashed with residents protesting the demolition of their homes, leaving nearly 10 people injured, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the clashes . Similar confrontations occurred in Wabari, where government forces used live ammunition against residents resisting eviction, and in Daynile, where rival security factions clashed over demolitions in the Warlaliska neighbourhood. The Heritage Institute report attributes the crisis in part to a governance vacuum. The Benadir Regional Administration and the Ministry of Public Works dispute responsibility for urban land, creating what the report describes as an opening for “predatory political and commercial elites” to enrich themselves at the public’s expense. Developers use administrative decrees to acquire valuable land without competitive tendering or verification of ownership, and connected buyers rely on state security forces to evict occupants. The Union of Somali Islamic Scholars Councils intervened in August 2026, calling on the government to halt demolitions and investigate land seizures. The scholars said they had received complaints from residents who claimed to possess legal ownership documents but had their property challenged, seized, or subjected to fees with no clear legal basis, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the scholars’ intervention . What the Airport Plan Does Not Say Authorities have not disclosed the number of structures affected by the airport clearance plan, the specific neighbourhoods targeted, or the timeline for the proposed relocation and demolition exercise. The lack of detail leaves residents in the vicinity of the airport facing uncertainty about whether their homes or businesses will be affected, and what compensation or resettlement arrangements, if any, will be offered. Historical precedent offers little reassurance. In 2010, Somali security agents demolished approximately 500 homes near the airport, citing fears that they could be used as cover for insurgent attacks. Hundreds of families were left without shelter, and a BBC reporter at the time noted there was no evidence the government provided the land it had promised and Somali Political Elites ended up benefiting from the projects and building villas in the cleared area near the airport.. Critical Note The security rationale for clearing the airport buffer zone is genuine. Aden Adde serves as Somalia’s principal international gateway, and its proximity to densely populated areas increases the risk of collateral damage from any attack. A major security incident at the airport would be devastating for the government’s credibility and for the country’s connections to the outside world. But the government’s approach to land clearance in Mogadishu has a documented history that makes skepticism reasonable. The Heritage Institute’s findings, the pattern of violent confrontations in Tookiyo, Wabari, and Daynile, and the scholars’ intervention all point to the same conclusion: demolitions and evictions in the capital have too often served private interests rather than public ones. If the airport clearance follows the same pattern, it risks becoming another chapter in a land crisis that has already displaced more than two million people. The government has not yet published the details of this plan. Until it does, the residents of the airport zone have no way of knowing what will happen to them, and the public has no way of assessing whether the security benefits justify the human costs. The minister’s meeting produced a directive. It did not produce accountability, transparency, or a compensation framework. Those are the elements that would distinguish a legitimate security measure from another episode of state-enabled land capture. Share your story. They include families fleeing conflict in Baidoa, house demolitions by the Somali government in Mogadishu, and drought in their home areas. advertisements The new arrivals say they have received no reception support, shelter, or other forms of aid. Some are staying with relatives already struggling to make ends meet, while others have settled on their own on vacant land in Dadaab’s Ifo-2 camp. They lack food, housing, toilets and other basic services. Nurto Mohamed Ali, who arrived in Ifo-2 on 20 August, said her family had received no assistance and was struggling to meet basic needs. She is staying with relatives who arrived earlier. “Neighbours collect maize and cooking oil for us. That is how we are surviving now,” she said. “We have children who need food and bedding, but we have nothing to give them.” Nurto fled ongoing conflict in Baidoa between federal government forces and those loyal to the former South West State administration. She was a farmer raising her family on their two-hectare plot of land in Baidoa. Separated from her husband, she receives no support from him and is the sole income earner. In the refugee camp now, her seven children often go to bed hungry because she lacks food. They occupy a shelter made from plastic sheets, cloth and thorny branches in the yard of a relatives’ home – a household of 10. The days reach a scorching 37°C and the rainy season has begun. Nurto and her older children have to sleep outside without bedding while the youngest children cram themselves into the hut. Nurto said they had expected to receive assistance on arrival, including refugee registration cards, household items, and a house. She has received nothing. “We have no proper house, and even the people who arrived before us do not have one. The shelter situation is very difficult. We sleep on pieces of cloth and a small, broken mat,” she said. Other vulnerable new arrivals, including older people, people with disabilities, women and children, are finding no formal help in the camp, where some walk around daily asking more established residents for food. Hawo Mohamed Ali, her disabled husband, and their 10 children arrived in Ifo-2 on 1 August. They fled Mogadishu’s Hodan district after the government demolished their house, saying the land belonged to the state. They had lived in the house for 34 years without having formal land ownership documents. She said losing the home made it impossible for her family to remain in Mogadishu. “When we left and went outside, we found our land fenced off and surrounded by a wall,” she told Radio Ergo. “We were told the land would be measured and returned to us. Our houses were demolished using bulldozers, and we thought the land would be given back. Later, we were told it was government land and that we had to leave.” The demolition left Hawo’s family homeless and they decided their only option was to seek refuge in Dadaab. In Mogadishu, she earned a living selling meat and watermelon in local markets. In the refugee camp, however, they have not been registered and haven’t received aid cards or assistance. She looked for laundry work, but the jobs are irregular, so she has to ask others for help with food for her children. She lacks firewood and containers for collecting water. “The children’s father is disabled, and life is very difficult for us. My children are still young and have nothing here. We left our home and came to a place we do not know,” said Hawo, adding that the conditions in Dadaab were far worse than she had expected. The chairman of Hagardera camp, Khalif Dhubow Jelle, said the hardship facing new arrivals from Somalia had been brought to the attention of humanitarian agencies in the camps, but no effective response had followed. He recorded nearly 250 families having arrived from southern Somalia in the past three months. “Their living conditions are extremely poor. It is also the rainy season, yet these people have no shelter or place to stay. They are sitting in the open and have no food or water,” he said. The new arrivals are joining a refugee population already struggling with difficult living conditions because of reduced humanitarian aid and wider economic hardship across the camps. somalia.summary: Families fleeing crises in Somalia are facing dire conditions in the Dadaab refugee camps in Kenya. The camps, originally established to accommodate a temporary influx of refugees, are now home to over 200,000 people, leading to overcrowding and limited resources. Many refugees are struggling with inadequate access to food, clean water, and healthcare. The ongoing conflict, drought, and famine in Somalia have driven families to seek safety, but the camps offer little hope for a better future. Aid organizations are overwhelmed and unable to meet the growing needs of the population, leaving many refugees in a state of uncertainty and despair. The situation highlights the urgent need for international support and sustainable solutions to address the challenges faced by displaced families.

In his meeting with Speaker of the House of the People, Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur (Jaamac), the discussions focused on enhancing cooperation between the Somali parliament and the EU’s legislative bodies. The goal is to strengthen the capacity of the House of the People and expand the exchange of knowledge and expertise. Speaker Nur thanked the European Union for its continued support for Somalia in the fields of security and state-building, emphasizing the importance of further solidifying the partnership between the two sides. Engaging the Upper House In a parallel meeting on the same day, Ambassador Máthé met with Speaker of the Upper House Abdi Hashi Abdullahi. That discussion centered on the EU’s ongoing support for infrastructure development and Somalia’s various government institutions. Máthé confirmed that the EU will continue its support for development projects across both the federal government and the Federal Member States. The two officials also discussed the general situation in the country, electoral matters, and opportunities to strengthen cooperation and improve the work of the Upper House. A Comprehensive Diplomatic Push Meeting both speakers on the same day reflects a deliberate strategy by the new EU envoy to establish a comprehensive relationship with Somalia’s federal legislative branch. The EU has long been one of Somalia’s most significant partners, with engagement spanning security, governance, and development. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of EU security support , the bloc approved a €75 million contribution to the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) in April 2026, maintaining its position as the mission’s largest financial supporter. The EU also supports Somali security forces through EUTM Somalia. On the political front, the EU has been closely engaged with Somalia’s constitutional review and electoral transition. In May 2026, Justice Minister Hassan Moallim Mahmoud met with EU ambassadors to discuss the completion of the provisional constitution and the government’s push toward a one-person, one-vote system, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the constitutional talks . However, the bloc has also expressed concerns about the political impasse. The EU’s diplomatic service publicly urged Somalia’s political actors in June to de-escalate, respect the constitutional order, and refrain from unilateral actions regarding the electoral process, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the EU’s call for dialogue . Critical Note Ambassador Máthé’s dual meetings with Speakers Nur and Abdi Hashi are routine diplomatic engagements, but they take place at a moment when the Somali parliament’s legitimacy is deeply contested. The House of the People recently approved constitutional amendments extending the presidential term, a move the opposition has challenged in the Supreme Court. The Upper House is the chamber through which those amendments passed. When the EU ambassador discusses “institutional capacity” and “exchange of knowledge” with the speakers of these chambers, he is engaging with institutions that the opposition views as compromised. The EU has positioned itself as a steadfast supporter of the federal government, funding security missions and budget support tied to governance reforms. Its Partnership Dialogue framework explicitly links continued engagement to progress on democratisation, rule of law, and inclusive political processes. The challenge for Máthé is to reconcile the EU’s support for Somalia’s institutions with its stated commitment to democratic principles. Engaging the speakers is necessary, but it is not sufficient. If the EU’s support for parliamentary capacity-building proceeds without corresponding pressure for an inclusive electoral process, it risks being perceived as endorsing the very institutional capture that the opposition decries. The ambassador’s next steps will determine whether the EU’s engagement is seen as a genuine partnership or as a diplomatic rubber stamp.
